item.content:encoded:
French policing under scrutiny as student protest injuries mount Reuters | Updated: 10-10-2026 11:30 IST | Created: 10-10-2026 11:30 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

By Juliette Jabkhiro and Layli Foroudi PARIS/ARGENTEUIL, France, Oct 10 (Reuters) - F ourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said. The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face. "(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said. A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. According to the prosecutor’s office, the police officer said that he was seeking to protect himself and his colleagues after the student confronted police. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident. The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of student unrest over conditions in schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades. The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate. It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated discontent with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election. Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback. In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off — likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who paused the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case. Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said. Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors. “France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims — we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. “It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said. CALLS TO BAN 'LESS LETHAL' WEAPONS Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades. Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche. In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added. A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye. “He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said. The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets. The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden. Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security. “We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party told Reuters. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police. Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions. “How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”

item.content:encoded:
Cricket-New Zealand's O'Rourke ruled out of India series Reuters | Updated: 10-10-2026 11:23 IST | Created: 10-10-2026 11:23 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

New Zealand fast-bowler Will O'Rourke will miss the series against India as he continues his rehabilitation from injuries to his left hamstring and calf, the country's cricket board said on Saturday. O'Rourke suffered a hamstring tear during New Zealand's test series win over England in June, before hurting his calf in training in late August. The 25-year-old will aim to return to full fitness ahead of a four-test tour of neighbours Australia beginning on December 9. "It's obviously disappointing for Will to have to miss such a marquee tour at home against India," New Zealand coach Rob Walter said in a statement. "He was set to feature in both the ODI and test series, but following subsequent discussions, we all agreed it was best for him to take some more time to rehabilitate both injuries and safely build up his bowling loads. "Our pace bowling resources will be critical over the next few months so we're taking a conservative approach to Will's return to ensure he's fully fit before he takes the field again." New Zealand host India in five Twenty20 internationals, five one-day internationals and two tests, with the opening T20 in Christchurch on October 22.

NEWSMAKER-Pressure mounts on India poll chief Gyanesh Kumar over voter list changes Reuters | Updated: 10-10-2026 10:33 IST | Created: 10-10-2026 10:33 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India's "Cockroach" youth movement and opposition parties are pushing hard for election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign over accusations of widespread manipulation of voter lists during an exercise to verify one billion voters. The calls come a month after US President Donald Trump praised the former bureaucrat, who took over as India's chief election commissioner in February 2025, for insisting that voters prove their identity with photo ID, unlike in the US. Criticism of Kumar, who has denied all accusations, soared last month after a report in the Indian Express newspaper. The paper said his two deputies had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions regarding voter rolls, registration procedures and the poll body's digital systems. Election Commission data shows that more than 130 million names, a figure exceeding the population of Japan, have been struck off the voter list since the latest round of revisions began last year. Nearly 650 million people of the 960 million registered voted in the last general election in 2024. The opposition has long claimed that the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage and was quick to repeat the accusations after the Indian Express report. Government ministers, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the poll body have all denied the charges. Kumar, 62, and the two other election commissioners have not commented, but the Election Commission said, "Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution". PROTEST THREAT The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has called a protest in New Delhi on Saturday to demand Kumar's resignation, and the main opposition alliance led by the Congress party has also staged protests this week calling for him to step down. Kumar has defended the actions of the poll body and told a press conference last year: "For the Election Commission, there is neither an opposition nor a ruling side; everyone is equal." When Trump praised him, Kumar was riding high in sections of the Indian media last month. But since the Indian Express report, graffiti have appeared near his ancestral home in northern India calling him a traitor. Kumar joined the Indian Administrative Service in 1988 after completing his B.Tech in civil engineering from an elite government college in his northern home state of Uttar Pradesh. He previously worked in the defence and home ministries, and retired in January 2024. Two months later he was appointed an election commissioner, before eventually becoming the chief. Kumar has had a troubled relationship with opposition parties from the start of his tenure as chief. Opposition lawmakers presented a motion in parliament for his removal this year, but it was rejected.
